claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by the degree of short-range chemical ordering induced by changes in Al content.
The balance of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation resistance, and cryogenic toughness is governed by short-range chemical ordering.
Moderate increases in Al promote B2-type ordered regions within a primarily disordered matrix.
B2-type ordered regions improve high-temperature strength relative to a lower-Al disordered baseline.
B2-type ordered regions improve performance under irradiation relative to a lower-Al disordered baseline.
B2-type ordered regions reduce cryogenic toughness relative to a lower-Al disordered baseline.
Systematically increasing Al while holding the Co:Cr:Fe:Ni ratio constant can be used to cross an ordering-transition boundary.
Increasing Al promotes local chemical ordering, especially between Al and Ni.
Al–Ni chemical ordering locally lowers free energy and stabilizes B2-type precipitates.
B2-type ordered regions impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion enhances high-temperature strength.
B2-type ordered regions act as defect sinks.
The intrinsic brittleness of the ordered regions reduces cryogenic toughness.

Moderate-Al alloys will exhibit a measurable B2-ordered volume fraction, higher elevated-temperature yield strength, improved post-irradiation defect resistance, and lower cryogenic impact or fracture toughness than the low-Al baseline.
The hypothesis may not apply at extreme Al contents or under non-equilibrium processing.
The Al threshold for optimal B2 ordering and the quantitative property trade-offs are uncertain and may depend on processing details.
Failure of increasing Al to produce consistent B2 ordering or the predicted property pattern relative to the low-Al baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
